title: The computational universe
question: Does Wolfram's 2002 account give Zuse's computational-universe proposal the credit warranted by its relationship to Wolfram's work?

usual_credit.summary: Stephen Wolfram's 2002 book A New Kind of Science studies simple computational rules and their possible relevance to fundamental physics. Its [historical notes](https://www.wolframscience.com/reference/notes/1026b/) name Zuse and Fredkin, so the disputed credit is not an unqualified claim that Wolfram first imagined a computational universe. Wolfram distinguishes literal cellular-automaton models from the more abstract models he proposes as an eventual account of physics. The book's scientific program and presentation of earlier work are at issue, not an experimentally established discovery that the universe is a computer.

works.title: A New Kind of Science, Chapter 9 and historical notes on mechanistic models

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that Zuse had already proposed a discrete computational universe in 1967 and expanded the proposal in Rechnender Raum in 1969. He objects that Wolfram's historical note describes Zuse's idea as a continuous cellular automaton, which he considers a misleading distinction from Wolfram's own program. His criticism concerns attribution and novelty, not experimental proof that Zuse's physical hypothesis is correct.

response.summary: Wolfram's [historical note](https://www.wolframscience.com/reference/notes/1026b/) explicitly acknowledges Zuse and Fredkin, but distinguishes their literal mechanistic proposals from the approach developed in his book. He argues that the ultimate models need not have the immediately recognizable structure of classical cellular automata. This gives a substantive reason for treating the book as a separate program despite earlier computational-universe proposals. The note is the 2002 position under criticism, rather than a later reply to Schmidhuber, and whether it accurately describes Zuse's model remains a separate attribution question.

quotes.text: no such literal mechanistic model can ever in the end realistically be expected to work.

agreed_facts: Zuse's Rechnender Raum appeared as a book in 1969 and has a 1970 English translation: https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Zuse-CalculatingSpace.pdf
Wolfram's A New Kind of Science was published in 2002 and its historical note names Zuse and Fredkin: https://www.wolframscience.com/reference/notes/1026b/
Schmidhuber's online criticism identifies itself as based on a CERN Courier letter from June 2003: https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/wolfram.html
crux: The issue is whether the computational-universe proposal and the scientific program presented by Wolfram are the same contribution, and whether his historical note fairly represents Zuse. An earlier speculation and a later program can share a broad idea without every model, method or novelty claim being identical.

card.headline: Computational universe
card.question: Does Wolfram's 2002 book give Zuse's computational-universe idea the credit it deserves?
card.claim: He says Zuse first proposed in 1967 that the universe is computed on a discrete computer, and that Wolfram's note misrepresents Zuse's model.
card.pushback: Wolfram's book names Zuse and Fredkin, and argues that literal cellular-automaton models like theirs cannot work, unlike his more abstract models.
card.crux: The question is whether Zuse's 1967 proposal and Wolfram's 2002 program are the same contribution, and whether Wolfram describes Zuse fairly.
